topic.subject: science
topic.title: Health and disease
topic.scope: health vs disease, acute and chronic, infectious agents, modes of spread, prevention, immunisation

misconceptions.statement: Being healthy means simply not having any visible illness.
misconceptions.why: Students often equate the absence of symptoms with a state of complete well-being.
misconceptions.fix: Health is a state of physical, mental, and social well-being, not just the absence of disease.

probe.question: If a person has no fever or pain but is constantly stressed and socially isolated, are they healthy?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because they do not have a disease.

misconceptions.statement: Health is purely a personal matter independent of the environment.
misconceptions.why: Students focus on individual hygiene and diet, ignoring the role of community surroundings.
misconceptions.fix: Personal health depends on the surrounding environment, including clean water, sanitation, and social harmony.

probe.question: Can you be perfectly healthy if you live in a neighborhood with open sewage and garbage?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, as long as I eat healthy food and stay clean.

misconceptions.statement: All chronic diseases are infectious and spread from person to person.
misconceptions.why: Students often conflate the severity of a disease with its ability to spread.
misconceptions.fix: Chronic diseases like diabetes or asthma are long-term conditions that are usually non-infectious.

probe.question: Can you catch diabetes from sitting next to a classmate who has it?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it is a long-lasting disease.

misconceptions.statement: All microbes are harmful and cause diseases.
misconceptions.why: Textbooks often introduce microbes in the context of illness, ignoring beneficial ones.
misconceptions.fix: Many microbes are harmless or even beneficial to humans, such as those in our gut.

probe.question: Are all bacteria found in the human body dangerous?

misconceptions.statement: Diseases are spread only through direct physical touch.
misconceptions.why: Students rely on visible contact as the primary mechanism for transmission.
misconceptions.fix: Diseases can spread through indirect means like contaminated water, food, air droplets, or vectors like mosquitoes.

probe.question: How can someone get malaria if they never touched a sick person?
probe.wrong_answer: They cannot get it because they didn't touch anyone.

misconceptions.statement: Vaccines give you the disease they are meant to prevent.
misconceptions.why: Students misunderstand the concept of using weakened or dead pathogens to trigger an immune response.
misconceptions.fix: Vaccines train the immune system to recognize and fight pathogens without causing the actual disease.

probe.question: Why do doctors give polio drops to healthy children?
probe.wrong_answer: To give them a small amount of polio so they get sick and recover.
